title: Block close: the great conversation
hookLine: two thousand years of thinkers arguing, praying and adding

lines: STEP BACK AND SEE THE WHOLE TABLE.
cards: A long table, and the chairs keep filling. At one end, Justin, a teacher in Rome, says the seeds of the Word were scattered everywhere, even among the philosophers. Further down, Augustine confesses to God out loud.
Boethius talks with Philosophy in his cell. Anselm tries to think the greatest thing that can be thought. Julian of Norwich, quietly: all shall be well.
Luther bangs the table about grace. Pascal mutters about reasons of the heart. Kierkegaard insists on the single person.
Bonhoeffer writes questions from prison. At the near end, the newest arrivals: a priest-physicist, a teacher from the rice fields, a scholar from Kenya. Nobody here agrees about everything.

teach.b: Some call it the great conversation, centuries long. Four things stand out. First, they argued.
Anselm built an argument; others pushed back. Aquinas set out his five ways; Ockham shaved away what he thought wasn't needed. Luther and the Catholic thinkers who answered him disagreed deeply.
Second, they prayed. Augustine wrote his Confessions as a long prayer. Dionysius climbed a ladder of names into silence.
Simone Weil said attention, at its highest, is prayer. For several of them, thinking about God and talking to God were one act.
Third, they added. Nobody started from zero. Newman said doctrine grows, like a seed into a tree.
Ware handed on the Orthodox way. Mbiti and Koyama asked what the gospel sounds like in their own soil.
The letter to the Hebrews pictures the faithful of the past as a crowd in the stands: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight."
Fourth, they never finished. The preacher in Ecclesiastes warned, a little wearily: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh."

The books kept coming anyway, and so did the conversation. That's the good news of an unfinished table: there's still a chair. Anyone who reads, asks, doubts, prays, or writes in a margin is already taking part.

how: Christians read the great thinkers of their tradition in study groups, seminaries and on their own, often keeping a favorite writer for years.

o: a church service that ends a week of fasting
the end of a run of lessons, with a look back
a final exam on everything learned so far

s: the great Christian thinkers all agreed with one another
they argued: Anselm and his critics, Aquinas and Ockham, Luther and his Catholic answerers.
Augustine wrote his Confessions as a prayer, addressed to God
the Confessions speak to God throughout.

games.q: you've just spent weeks with the great thinkers. so many voices, so much disagreement. what do you do?
o: decide it's too much and put it all away.
pick the one whose question is also yours and keep reading.
choose the one everyone says is the most important.
games.why: the block ends here: notice the one you keep returning to and pull up a chair. the table is unfinished, and there's room.

practice: Let the faces of this block pass by, Augustine, Boethius, Julian, Aquinas, Luther, Pascal, Wesley, Kierkegaard, Bonhoeffer, Weil, Merton, Ware, Koyama, Mbiti, Polkinghorne and the rest, and notice the one whose question is also yours, not the one you think you should choose.
Let that one take a seat beside you. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, just hold their question for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of the great thinkers: people who argued, prayed and added, around a table that still has room.

carryVoice: Your line: join the conversation. Centuries of voices, and room for one more. And that closes the block.
